name: ngrep
why: Greps live network traffic by pattern, a direct window into the packets your machine sends and receives all day.

brief.what_it_is: ngrep is a command-line packet sniffer that works like GNU grep applied to network traffic. You give it a regular expression (or a hexadecimal pattern with -X) and an optional BPF filter, and it captures live packets through libpcap or reads a saved pcap file. It prints the packets whose payloads match, with source and destination addresses, and it can also write matched traffic to a dump file with -O. It understands IPv4/6, TCP, UDP, ICMPv4/6, IGMP and raw packets.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says ngrep was originally built to debug plaintext protocols such as HTTP, IMAP, DNS and SIP, to analyze suspicious traffic such as malware communications, and to search and reprocess pcap dump files for specific data patterns. The README also notes it could be used to collect plaintext credentials, and adds that 'Like all useful tools, it can be used for good and for bad.'
brief.how_it_works: It uses libpcap to capture packets from one or more interfaces, and BPF filter syntax (the same kind tcpdump uses) to limit what is captured. Each packet payload is then matched against the given extended regex or hex expression, and matches are printed with addresses and flags. The README says PCRE2 is the default on macOS/Homebrew and Windows builds, while GNU regex is the other option.

commands_seen.context: README's first suggested install route: pulls the official container image from GitHub Container Registry.
README example: runs ngrep in Docker with host networking and the NET_RAW capability, quietly matching GET or POST on TCP port 80.
EXAMPLES.md: monitors all traffic on source or destination port 25 (SMTP) across every interface, using 'any' as the device.
EXAMPLES.md: watches FTP traffic on port 21 for the words 'user' or 'pass', case-insensitively and matched as whole words.
EXAMPLES.md: HTTP sniffing with -W byline so embedded line feeds are respected and headers are easier to read.
EXAMPLES.md: captures DNS traffic to a dump file with -O while printing time differences with -T.
EXAMPLES.md: -X treats the match as a hex pattern and -x prints matched packets in hex, for finding binary content in web traffic.
EXAMPLES.md: with -r, container names replace raw IPs in the output, shown here on the docker0 bridge watching Postgres traffic.
EXAMPLES.md: shows HTTP requests on a Docker Compose bridge network with container names in place of IPs.
EXAMPLES.md: watches DNS lookups between containers, using an empty match expression to match every packet.

brief.install_notes: Easiest route per the README is Docker: docker pull ghcr.io/jpr5/ngrep:latest, then run with --net=host and --cap-add=NET_RAW. Pre-built binaries are on the GitHub Releases page. Building from source is described in an INSTALL file, which I did not open. Container name resolution (-r) is compiled in by default and can be turned off at build time with --disable-container-resolution. For -r, if the Docker or Podman socket is reachable, ngrep uses the Events API; otherwise it falls back to CLI polling with a 30-second cache. The README does not spell out a sudo or privilege requirement for plain host use.
brief.standout: The -r flag resolves Docker and Podman container IPs to container names in live output, so a capture reads as api_gateway talking to postgres_db rather than a bare 172.18.x address. It also keeps the classic grep-style pattern plus BPF filter model, so the same expression works on a live interface or a saved pcap.
brief.status: Maintained, by the evidence available. The README header reads 'ngrep 1.49.0 (2.7.2026)' with a 'What's New' list that includes recent Windows ARM64 and PCRE2 work, and there is a build badge pointing at GitHub Actions. I did not see a commit date. The date format in the header is ambiguous, so I cannot give an exact release date.
brief.caveats: The 'Working Platforms' list is a historical one, from Linux 2.0 and Solaris 2.5.1 to Windows 10, and the README points to the autobuild matrix for current support. Regex library choice changes the license: GNU regex means GPL, PCRE2 means BSD-style, per the README. The Docker example needs host networking and NET_RAW. Container filtering still uses raw IPs, so you look up a container's IP with docker inspect before filtering. Without a Docker or Podman socket (rootless Podman, permission issues), -r falls back to polling. The author also asks distribution maintainers to CC him on bug reports and patches, because he often finds out late.
quotes: ngrep is like GNU grep applied to the network layer.
Like all useful tools, it can be used for good and for bad.
at the end of the day it's my code, so it's my responsibility, but I can't be everywhere to see everything.
fetch_log: https://github.com/jpr5/ngrep/blob/master/EXAMPLES.md (worked; GitHub page wrapper is noisy but the examples text is readable)

judge.reason: Applying grep patterns directly to live packets and pcaps makes everyday protocols inspectable, with BPF filters and container-name resolution adding useful depth.

entry.title: ngrep
entry.tldr: ngrep is grep for the network: give it a regex and a filter, and it prints live packets whose payloads match.
entry.deeper_look:
ngrep captures packets through libpcap, either live from an interface or from a saved pcap file. It matches each payload against an extended regular expression, or a hex pattern with `-X`, and prints the matches with addresses and flags. It understands IPv4 and IPv6, TCP, UDP, ICMP, IGMP and raw packets. The same filter syntax tcpdump uses (BPF) narrows what gets captured in the first place.

The author built it to debug plaintext protocols such as HTTP, IMAP, DNS and SIP, to look at suspicious traffic like malware communications, and to search pcap dumps for particular patterns. The README is frank that it could also collect plaintext credentials, and adds: "Like all useful tools, it can be used for good and for bad."

The idea underneath is that a packet is just bytes with a header, and you already know how to search bytes. Pointing `grep` thinking at port 25 or port 21 shows how much of the network still travels as readable text. It also shows why that is a problem.

The `-r` flag resolves Docker and Podman container IPs to container names. A capture on a bridge network then reads as one service talking to another, not as a list of 172.18.x addresses.
entry.install:
brew install ngrep
# Capturing packets usually needs elevated privileges on the host, so you may need sudo. The README does not spell this out.
# Alternative per the README: docker pull ghcr.io/jpr5/ngrep:latest

try_this.what_happens: Shows plain HTTP traffic with line breaks respected, so headers are readable.
Captures DNS traffic on every interface into a dump file, printing time differences between packets.
Watches DNS lookups between containers, matching every packet, with container names in place of IPs.

entry.whats_unique: It keeps the grep model of pattern plus filter, and the `-r` flag turns Docker and Podman container IPs into names in live output. The same expression works on a live interface or a saved pcap.
entry.caveats: Only plaintext payloads are readable, so most modern HTTPS traffic will show nothing useful, and the Docker route needs host networking plus the NET_RAW capability.
